newsitem.title: USA: Procter & Gamble posts record profit despite lower sales.
newsitem.headline: Procter & Gamble posts record profit despite lower sales.

text.p: Procter & Gamble Co. Thursday said profits rose to nearly $1 billion in the latest quarter, beating expectations on Wall Street, but its stock tumbled on investor disappointment with the company's sales overseas.

The nation's largest consumer products company said net income for its fiscal first quarter ended on Sept. 30 rose to $979 million, or $1.39 a share, from $896 million or $1.27 a share, in the 1995 quarter.

But the maker of Tide detergent, Crest toothpaste, Pampers disposable diapers and other products said that despite record unit sales volume worldwide, sales for the quarter slipped to $8.90 billion from $9.03 billion, mainly because of the strong dollar compared with other currencies.
Worries about sales declines, especially in important markets in Latin America and Asia, sparked a steep decline in Procter & Gamble's stock.
P&G stock lost $2.25 to close at $94 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was one of the most active issues.
Per-share results were 2 cents better than Wall Street estimates of $1.37, according to First Call, which tracks analysts' estimates.
Excluding the effect of unfavourable exchange rates, particularly in Japan and Germany, sales increased consistent with unit volume growth, the company said.

The Cincinnati-based company, which also makes Ivory soap, Comet, and Hawaiian Punch drinks, said its North America shipments, led by laundry and cleaning products, grew 2 percent to a new record as dollar sales rose 1 percent.
P&G said sales and volume increased despite capacity constraints on some fast-growing categories, such as tissues and towels.
The company said unit sales volume in Europe, Middle East and Africa grew 5 percent to a record, but unit volumes were down 9 percent in Asia and 6 percent in Latin America.

Analysts said the declines in Asia and Latin America unnerved investors and caused the sell-off. But they said they expected problems to be short-lived and remained positive about the consumer products giant's long-term outlook.
"Worldwide volume was up 1 percent," Amy Low, an analyst with Goldman Sachs, said, adding she plans to keep the stock on her recommended list.

"Some volumes in foreign markets were off more than expected, but it's something that should iron itself out over the next few quarters," said Wesley Roberts, an analyst with J.J.B. Hilliard, L.W. Lyons.
William Steele, an analyst with Dean Witter Reynolds, said good cost controls aided earnings.

"The company is doing what they have to do from a long-term perspective," he said. "(P&G is) leveraging their inherent strengths, which are strong products, great brand promotion and a lean cost structure."
